what_its_for: Tucatinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of breast cancer called HER2-positive breast cancer. It is used in adults whose cancer has spread to other parts of the body (including the brain) and who have already tried other HER2 treatments. It is always used together with two other medicines called trastuzumab (Herceptin) and capecitabine (Xeloda).
how_to_take: Swallow the tablets whole with or without food. Do not crush, cut, or chew the tablets. Take your doses about 12 hours apart (for example, 8 AM and 8 PM) every day. Try to take it at the same times each day to help you remember. If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take another dose — just take your next scheduled dose at the regular time.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 300 mg (two 150 mg tablets) taken by mouth twice a day, approximately 12 hours apart. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different based on your health and other medicines you take.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if your next scheduled dose is more than 6 hours away. If your next dose is less than 6 hours away, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once or extra doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tucatinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep out of the reach of children and pets. Do not store in the bathroom. Do not use tablets past the expiration date on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking certain medicines that can interact with tucatinib, including some antibiotics, antifungals, seizure medicines, and HIV medications — always tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking this medicine. Avoid becoming pregnant, as tucatinib can harm an unborn baby. Women should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 week after the last dose. Men with female partners who could become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for 1 week after stopping.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: severe diarrhea (more than 4 loose stools per day or diarrhea with fever), signs of liver problems (yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, stomach pain, unusual tiredness), severe rash or skin blistering, signs of heart problems (shortness of breath, swelling in legs or ankles, fast heartbeat), signs of infection (fever, chills, cough), severe nausea or vomiting that stops you from eating, or if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
when_it_works: Tucatinib starts working right away to fight cancer cells, but it may take several weeks to months before you or your doctor can tell if the treatment is helping. Your doctor will do regular tests (blood tests and scans) to check how well the medicine is working. Keep taking your medicine as directed even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use tucatinib if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm your baby. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 1 week after the last dose. Liver problems: If you have moderate to severe liver disease, your doctor may adjust your dose. Tell your doctor about any history of liver problems. Kidney problems: No dose change is usually needed for mild to moderate kidney disease, but tell your doctor if you have kidney problems. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children.
